misses.text:
Founderism: The Four Questions

In every community there was somebody who took the initiative to get it started. Somebody had to find the land, write the first documents, teach the method, recruit the first members, or even just keep things going when others lost interest.

That person ends up with real influence, and pretending they don't just makes that influence harder to look at.

I know this tension personally. Many of the methods discussed in this article were my doing, and I wrote the materials, so it would be very easy for me to become someone who could decide whether or not everyone else “understood” them correctly. Writing in an anti-authoritarian way does not keep the author from enjoying being an author.

A few things help. One is to judge the method by results people can actually see. Are the members flourishing, and are they safe? Can conflicts get resolved? Can people disagree, leave, and later tell a different story about it? Are the kids doing well once they grow up? Is the community still materially viable? Can it correct a prediction that turned out wrong? Can it replace the founder? And if it's meant to spread, do new projects actually start up and last? How long a community has lasted, how full it is, whether it reaches consensus and how many members stay aren't enough on their own. A group can keep its members because people love it, or because leaving costs too much. And don't judge it by how closely people stick to the founder's own interpretation.

Allow for parallel implementations. Fork the method. If the community finds a way to alter Hearthwork and get better results, they've taught me something. If it needs the founder's “blessing”, then it's not really running in parallel, is it?

Here are the four questions:

Can the community override the founder, with all due respect? Can the community replace the role of the founder? Can the community alter the vision of the founder? Can the community exist without the founder?

Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who's in charge of the housing and the food stores, the vehicles and tools, and any bank account outside the community? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the reviewers? Who controls access to the kids, or to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart might look flat and horizontal, while the keys, passwords, titles and even just general reputation all point to one person.

An override is only real if it can actually work against the person being challenged. If the founder picks the reviewer, holds the records, owns the land, and can kick out whoever complained, the community can't really override the founder, no matter how many circles it holds.

Ask these questions about any community, teacher or method. And ask them about me, if people end up living on land I buy.

Also watch for the daily signs. Increasing focus on the founder over time. Sense that disagreement is failure. Bad results are blamed on lack of good implementation. Increasing “insider” knowledge. Decreasing public accountability. Failure to measure results. Sense that those who leave are morally contaminated.

Presence of one of these alone isn't proof of abuse, but if several are present, they are worth paying attention to before the founder can explain how the situation is uniquely different in a spiritual way.

How My Own Model Could Become a Cult

I could totally start a cult. Trust me.

Every practice in this article can be turned against the people using it.

“Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can turn into compulsory disclosure. I’ve seen that risk in communities that use ZEGG Forum. A group can start out inviting honesty and end up treating privacy as resistance.

Peer counseling can be turned into peer surveillance, even with a warm tone. Requiring practices like that as prerequisites for medicine can create gatekeepers who have power over people when they are most open. Even the idea of “willing to be seen” can be used to demand that people disclose to the group whatever the group wants them to.

The boundary is simple. These aren't things that give the community power over me, they are simply a set of principles I am attempting to live up to.

“Nothing suppressed” applies to myself and my relationship with my own material. It doesn't give anyone the right to pull anything out of me. Any member can choose not to share material, and they don't need to provide a therapeutic rationale for not sharing.

The medicine is optional. Choosing not to take the medicine in no way affects anyone's rights as a member. The right to let people into the group is not vested in any individual or permanent clique. And disagreement gets answered as disagreement.

“Your resistance is your wound talking” is pretty much a conversation ender. Once you notice a community diagnosing dissent like this instead of answering it, leave. Better yet, leave before it even gets to the point of people wanting to do group process about your leaving.

There are some basics that the majority should not be allowed to vote away from any member of a community. These basics include your bodily safety, adequate food and sleep, the right to go to a doctor of your choice, the right to keep your thoughts private, the right to communicate with people outside the community, the right to report harm without asking the accused person's friends for permission, the right to leave. Removing these rights from a community member is not consensual, even if a majority vote does it.

misses.text:
Founderism: The Four Questions

In every community there was somebody who took the initiative to get it started. Somebody found the land, wrote the first documents, taught the method, recruited the first members, or kept things going when everybody else lost interest.

That person ends up with real influence, and pretending they don't just makes that influence harder to look at.

I know this personally. Many of the methods discussed in this article were my doing, and I wrote the materials, so it would be very easy for me to become the person who decides whether or not everyone else “understood” them correctly. Writing in an anti-authoritarian way does not keep the author from enjoying being an author.

A few things help keep that in check. One is to judge the method by results people can actually see. Are the members flourishing, and are they safe? Can conflicts get resolved? Can people disagree, leave, and later tell a different story about it? Are the kids doing well once they grow up? Is the community still materially viable? Can it correct a prediction that turned out wrong? Can it replace the founder? And if it's meant to spread, do new projects actually start up and last? How long a community has lasted, how full it is, whether it reaches consensus and how many members stay aren't enough on their own. A group can keep its members because people love it, or because leaving costs too much. And don't judge it by how closely people stick to the founder's own interpretation.

Allow for parallel implementations. Fork the method. If the community finds a way to alter Hearthwork and get better results, they've taught me something. If every change still needs the founder's “blessing”, then the versions aren't really running in parallel, are they?

Here are the four questions about the founder:

Can the community respectfully override the founder? Can the community replace the role of the founder? Can the community alter the vision of the founder? Can the community exist without the founder?

Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who's in charge of the housing and the food stores, the vehicles and tools, and any bank account outside the community? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the reviewers? Who controls access to the kids, or to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart might look flat and horizontal, while the keys, passwords, titles and even just general reputation all point to one person.

Remember, it's not an override unless it can actually work on the person in question. If the founder selects the person to review the founder, holds the records, has title to the land, and can kick out complainers, then there's no way for the community to override the founder, no matter how many circles it holds.

Also watch for the daily signs. Increasing focus on the founder over time. Sense that disagreement is failure. Every bad result is blamed on lack of good implementation. Increasing “insider” knowledge while public accountability decreases. Results are never measured. Sense that former members become morally contaminated the moment they leave.

Presence of one of these alone isn't proof of abuse, but if several are present, they are worth paying attention to before the founder can explain how the situation is uniquely different in a spiritual way.

Ask these questions about any community, teacher or method. And ask them about me, if people end up living on land I buy.

While founderism is a problem in every community, it's especially so in communities which form naturally over time as I'm describing may happen in my case. In such cases, there's no formal community and no formal rules until people decide to come together to make them. It doesn't make sense to do that at first, if, say, I'm the only one there and I don't know who else will be there that I could trust. If there's one other person who comes to visit, it also doesn't make sense, so there's a critical mass point at which people decide "we were just living together like friends, but now we want to formalize the community."

If I could find a suitable commune to join, that would basically reverse this problem. I would then be the one on probation. But if we are all starting together from scratch, then we would all be at an equal probationary level with each other.

It's a bit like the process of getting married. At first, you visit your girlfriend or boyfriend when schedules align and each of you agrees. Over time as you get closer to marriage (which hopefully is not a fully unconscious process), you start making decisions together and considering sharing more and more resources. Once married, if you decide to divorce, you split up the resources, although that's also contentious depending on how long the marriage was for, whether one person feels tricked, etc,  and unfortunately often ends up in court.  Leaving a commune is the divorce half of it, where the shared resources have to get split up. When joining or forming a commune, we can hopefully be more conscious about the process and less romantic.

Friends who come to visit don't get written terms, though. That's not how anything works, and at first they don't even know if they'll stick around for a day or a week. There are implied terms, like be respectful and be honest, and those shouldn't need to be in writing. If someone is offered something like an internship or a probationary period, that would require written terms. Or if it naturally evolves and they bring up wanting something like that, it could be done.

How My Own Model Could Become a Cult

I could totally start a cult. Trust me.

Every practice in this article can be turned against the people using it.

“Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become a situation where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. A group starts out inviting honesty and ends up treating privacy as resistance. But privacy also can be resistance to the communal spirit, so there has to be a dynamic, living, always re-assessed balance between what you and the community owe each other, and what remains your own domain. In general, people can have their own private practices, of course. But some practices go too far against the communal spirit. If someone starts worshipping Satan, say, they get booted.

Peer counseling can become peer surveillance, even if the tone is warm. And when communal therapy processes are pre-reqs for people to get medicine or to be respected members, it can feel like the community is gatekeeping. Well, it is gatekeeping. Some people simply should not be let in the gate, at least not yet. And some people will resent that, and choose to leave, and that's fine. Some communities will be stricter gatekeepers, and others will be more lax. There are pros and cons to each extreme, and again, a living balance must be struck.

It should go without saying that nobody has to take medicine to have equal respect in the community. But medicine is an optional part of the overall therapy process, and if a member is avoiding the therapy process and becoming hard to deal with, they will naturally not belong at a certain point. If it gets to the point of being impossible to live with, they will be kicked out. But nearly always, people who don't fit in leave way before that.

They should not be demonized for not trying to fit in. They should be offered compassion, but ultimately it's up to them if they want to fit in and follow the communal processes. And in some cases, the community may make exceptions. If someone is actually sick and needs care, kicking them out could be like a death sentence. It depends on so many factors that I can't decide any of this ahead of time. It's up to the people involved.

No single person or permanent group of people should handle grievances and have the power to decide who gets into or stays in the community. Each person should have a usable avenue for exit. Dissent is important for growth. That doesn't mean everything everyone says is equally valid, though. Sometimes it really is their wounded ego projection, and that should be acknowledged. But again, balance, because if complaints are too often or too broadly painted as projection, that's as much a failure, if not more so.

There are some basic human rights that can’t be voted away from you by the majority in a community, unless it's a question of resource availability as a whole. If safety and the conditions for health can be provided, it should be provided. People should be able to maintain relationships with others outside the community, as long as those relationships don't interfere with the community as a whole (for example, you can't bring your boyfriend to live with you if he's not only not a member of the community, but also antagonistic towards it).

It can be tricky to spell everything out, though. Let's say a grandmother is demonizing the commune. Cutting off contact with her could make things way worse. When it's tricky and dangerous for everyone like that, I think the commune needs to step in and help people decide how to communicate with outsiders. Nobody can give that advice ahead of time, including me. It has to be worked out in the moment, context by context.

If your human rights are unfairly stripped from you, even by a majority vote, then you can vote with your feet.

Ask these questions about any community, teacher or method. And ask them about me, if people end up living on land I buy.

If there's one other person who comes to visit, it also doesn't make sense, so there's a critical mass point at which people decide "we were just living together like friends, but now we want to formalize the community."

If I could find a suitable commune to join, that would basically reverse this problem. I would then be the one on probation. But if we are all starting together from scratch, then we would all be at an equal probationary level with each other.

It's a bit like the process of getting married. At first, you visit your girlfriend or boyfriend when schedules align and each of you agrees. Over time as you get closer to marriage (which hopefully is not a fully unconscious process), you start making decisions together and considering sharing more and more resources. Once married, if you decide to divorce, you split up the resources, although that's also contentious depending on how long the marriage was for, whether one person feels tricked, etc,  and unfortunately often ends up in court.  Leaving a commune is the divorce half of it, where the shared resources have to get split up. When joining or forming a commune, we can hopefully be more conscious about the process and less romantic.

There are implied terms, like be respectful and be honest, and those shouldn't need to be in writing. In general, people can have their own private practices, of course. But some practices go too far against the communal spirit. If someone starts worshipping Satan, say, they get booted.

Peer counseling can become peer surveillance, even if the tone is warm. Some people simply should not be let in the gate, at least not yet. And some people will resent that, and choose to leave, and that's fine. Some communities will be stricter gatekeepers, and others will be more lax. There are pros and cons to each extreme, and again, a living balance must be struck.

It should go without saying that nobody has to take medicine to have equal respect in the community. But medicine is an optional part of the overall therapy process, and if a member is avoiding the therapy process and becoming hard to deal with, they will naturally not belong at a certain point. If it gets to the point of being impossible to live with, they will be kicked out. But nearly always, people who don't fit in leave way before that.

They should not be demonized for not trying to fit in. They should be offered compassion, but ultimately it's up to them if they want to fit in and follow the communal processes. And in some cases, the community may make exceptions. If someone is actually sick and needs care, kicking them out could be like a death sentence. It depends on so many factors that I can't decide any of this ahead of time. It's up to the people involved.

No single person or permanent group of people should handle grievances and have the power to decide who gets into or stays in the community. Each person should have a usable avenue for exit. Dissent is important for growth. That doesn't mean everything everyone says is equally valid, though. Sometimes it really is their wounded ego projection, and that should be acknowledged. But again, balance, because if complaints are too often or too broadly painted as projection, that's as much a failure, if not more so.

If your human rights are unfairly stripped from you, even by a majority vote, then you can vote with your feet.

misses.text:
The Math of Absorption, and Who This Isn’t For

I am asking people to talk about the core issues of life: jealousy, God, death, childhood, money, sex, psychedelics, and what happens when somebody wants to leave. The strange thing is, a lot of intelligent adults would much rather talk about solar panels for six hours.

This does not surprise me, since we are taught to put on a show of competence in modern society. We have a lot of incentives to hide ourselves in our lives and disappear behind our screens the second things get uncomfortable. We have been encouraged by our institutions to be narrow in our skills, and then they act surprised when nobody can sit through a conflict without appointing a subcommittee or blocking somebody.

So instead of asking "Is this person good enough?", some very practical questions to ask might be, "How much attention can this person bring to other people right now? How available is he or she to engage in self-examination? And how available are we to this person, without being consumed by him or her?"

Some people have engaged in long practices of contemplation or therapy, or have had very good luck in childhood; other people are just trying to survive some emergency in their life and need care more than responsibility. Most of us are all of these at different times in our lives.

In the model I’m imagining, some of the functions that are outsourced to therapists in modern society are distributed throughout the community. In other words, there’s a lot of peer counseling going on, people listening to each other and helping each other process ordinary emotional stuff.

But it’s not infinite.

I’m going to use the phrase “free resource,” which comes from Re-evaluation Counseling, to refer to the attention, steadiness and practical skill people have left over for others once they’ve dealt with enough of their own immediate stuff, and “need” to refer to the amount of help people need at a given time.

Everyone has a certain amount of both, and the ratio varies.

My own need has exceeded my free resource at many points. Good Lord. During one stretch, my first wife tried to kill me while psychotic because she believed I was her sociopathic father. Then she took my son. Later she tried to kill my mother, while her pimp stalked my sister’s family until they moved to Canada.

I could go on and on, but the math is pretty clear by now. There wasn’t much of me left over for anybody else. So when I say someone might need to stabilize and do inner pl/ork before helping found a community, I’m not saying it from a mountaintop.

A group can only absorb as much need as its members have free resource to meet. The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group may end up spending most of its attention caring for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the same need can often be spread across lots of relationships and roles.

So it’s partly a problem of resources, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?

There is a difficult paradox to consider. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to tolerate the disruption of new members is less. Even with only eight people in the community, someone still has to grow the food, fix the equipment, balance the books, watch the kids, and maintain the water system. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful a new member’s heart is.

Early on, members usually need to have more resource than need, and some skill to contribute, and a willingness to learn.

How to use the framing of “I don’t have the capacity to…” without it becoming a respectable way to exclude disabled people, poor people, less articulate people, people who don’t have the language of therapy at their fingertips, people who are simply not convenient – I don’t know. It’s not going to be solved by pretending it’s unlimited; that’s going to require actually making concrete criteria, allowing for outside review, allowing for re-visiting a “not now” decision, and all of that. And even then, the power is dangerous.

You want all of the benefits of village life but don’t want to take on governance, maintenance, conflict, care, etc.

You’re not willing to look at yourself when jealousy or conflict comes up.

You have a need that far outstrips your ability to bring in a resource for it right now. (This doesn’t mean you’re bad or doomed, it’s about timing; it may mean you need to take a first step of finding support where you are so you can build up your resources a bit.)
